notes:
I've written notes for every verse in John 2. Verses 1–11 have the most material, and verse 12 has a real disagreement worth covering. Verses 13–25 are thinner because the main commentary pages I opened were cut off partway through, and I ran out of searches before I could fill the gap. I also found nothing specifically Lutheran, Methodist or Orthodox, nothing from bibleodyssey.org, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter, so those are left out. "Guzik" below means David Guzik's commentary on enduringword.com.

---

**v. 1**
- **"On the third day":** One Precept Austin contributor thinks the phrase probably has no symbolic meaning. MacArthur takes it as the last of a series of time markers, so the events from John the Baptist's questioning to Cana fit into one week. Wiersbe makes it the seventh day of a "new creation week." https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
- **Mary's role:** Utley thinks Mary was apparently helping with the arrangements, since she gives orders to the servants and worries about the drinks. The family were probably relatives or friends. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2
- **Joseph's absence:** Barclay, quoted by Guzik, thinks Joseph had most likely died by then. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/

**v. 2**
- Guzik: this is the first of many stories showing that Jesus was always welcome among those having a good time. He quotes Spurgeon that Jesus blessing a marriage shows our family life is under his care. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- **Fringe view:** Guzik notes that a few Latter-day Saints and some New Age followers say this was Jesus' own wedding. He calls this against the plain meaning of the text. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/

**v. 3**
- Running out of wine was a serious social failure that could shame the couple for years (Tenney, quoted by Guzik). Morris adds that the hosts may have been poor and could even have faced legal liability. Guzik suggests Mary may have hoped Jesus would now show himself as Messiah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- Utley says it was a mandatory Hebrew custom for the guests to provide the wine. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2

**v. 4**
- **"Woman":** This was a respectful Hebrew way of speaking, not a harsh one (Utley). https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2 Guzik agrees it was respectful but notes Jesus did *not* call her "mother." He sees a new relationship beginning: Jesus' public work follows the Father's will, not family ties. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- **"My hour":** In John this usually points to Jesus' arrest, trial and death (Utley). https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2 Precept Austin reads it as the time when he would openly show who he is. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
- Deffinbaugh (bible.org) reads the reply as Jesus telling Mary she has no authority over him as her sovereign God. He also argues Jesus kept the miracle quiet so as to keep to the Father's timing. https://bible.org/seriespage/first-sign-jesus-turns-water-wine-john-21-11
- **Catholic reading:** Jesus is not objecting to the request, only questioning the timing. The hour of his saving death is the very basis of Mary's intercession. https://www.catholic.com/qa/didnt-jesus-tell-his-mother-that-she-was-out-of-line-in-trying-to-influence-him-at-cana Catholic writers also link "woman" to the woman of Genesis 3:15: Mary as the New Eve. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-new-adam-rebukes-the-new-eve One Catholic Answers podcast goes further and uses this to argue that Mary was sinless. https://www.catholic.com/audio/scw/marys-sinlessness-and-the-wedding-feast-at-cana-year-c
- **Protestant reply:** Guzik quotes Trench admitting that Catholic and Orthodox Christians have long seen this miracle as showing the value Jesus places on his mother's requests. Guzik says that misunderstands the passage. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/ Deffinbaugh calls the Catholic view "exaggerated." https://bible.org/seriespage/first-sign-jesus-turns-water-wine-john-21-11

**v. 5**
- Mary points the servants to Jesus, not to herself (Precept Austin). https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary Guzik notes that Mary's recorded words always glorify Jesus. He quotes Barnhouse that going through Mary to reach Jesus is foreign to the Bible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- Utley: Mary did not take Jesus' reply as a flat refusal. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2

**v. 6**
- The jars belong to the system of the Law, because they held water for ritual washing (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- Utley sees symbols here: six as the number of human effort, the jars filled to the brim, the huge amount, and wine as a sign of the new age. The "twenty or thirty gallons" is uncertain because there were three sizes of the measure used. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2
- **Caution:** The Precept Austin editor calls one such symbolic reading spiritualizing. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
- **Catholic:** the purification water stands for the "baptismal waters" of the Old Covenant, turned into the wine of the New. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-new-adam-rebukes-the-new-eve

**v. 7**
- Filled to the brim means Jesus was not adding to the water but transforming it. The servants obeyed fully and shared in the blessing (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- MacArthur: the full jars show nothing was added. The 120–180 gallons also displayed his generous grace and served as a wedding gift. https://shop.gty.org/library/bibleqnas-library/QA0124/why-would-jesus-create-wine

**v. 8**
- Taking it to the head waiter required faith from the servants. Jesus had the miracle tested straight away by the proper person (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/

**v. 9**
- Jesus spoke no words and used no ritual; he simply willed the change. The servants knew it was a miracle, while the head waiter knew only that it was good wine (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- Bible Hub's study notes link the wine to the cup Jesus later gave as the sign of his blood. https://biblehub.com/john/2-9.htm

**v. 10**
- Utley sees a contrast between the old covenant and the new, with the best saved for last. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2 Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, applies it to the believer finally seeing Christ face to face. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- **Real wine or not? Evangelicals differ:**
  - **Real, alcoholic wine:** GotQuestions says the Greek word means ordinary fermented wine. It calls the grape-juice reading unbiblical and says only misuse of alcohol is sin. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-water-wine.html Utley says the wine is obviously fermented. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2 Guzik says ordinary wine then was watered down and weaker than modern wine, but it was still wine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
  - **A different emphasis:** MacArthur calls it the sweetest, freshest wine, made from nothing rather than by fermentation. He adds that the steward's remark does not mean this feast had turned drunken. https://shop.gty.org/library/bibleqnas-library/QA0124/why-would-jesus-create-wine
  - **Total-abstinence view:** GotQuestions describes this view, held by those who oppose all drinking, before rejecting it. https://www.gotquestions.org/Jesus-water-wine.html
  - **Catholic:** the steward's comment shows the wine was alcoholic. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/the-use-of-alcohol

**v. 11**
- This is the first of seven signs around which John built his Gospel. Utley thinks "believed" here means the disciples' growing understanding, not their first act of faith. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2
- Guzik calls it a miracle of conversion, from Law and ritual to new life, and finds Jesus' glory in his compassion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- Carson (quoted by Precept Austin) advises asking how the story builds faith in Jesus. He says its rich theological themes do not weaken it as history. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
- **Critics answered:** Deffinbaugh describes a "liberal" view that no miracle happened (the guests simply played along with water) and rejects it. https://bible.org/seriespage/first-sign-jesus-turns-water-wine-john-21-11
- **Catholic:** it was through Mary's intercession that the disciples came to believe. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-new-adam-rebukes-the-new-eve

**v. 12**
- Capernaum became Jesus' base in Galilee (Utley). https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2
- **Who were "His brothers"? Protestants differ:**
  - **Physical brothers:** Constable says plainly that Jesus had physical brothers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/2-12.html Bible Hub's topical article also treats them as real brothers who did not yet understand him. https://biblehub.com/topical/b/brethren.htm
  - **Possibly cousins:** Calvin notes that in Hebrew "brethren" can mean cousins and other relatives. Gill (Baptist) calls them near kinsmen, sons of Alphaeus and of Mary's sister. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/2-12.html
  - **Catholic:** they were not Mary's children; the most common view is that they were cousins. https://www.catholic.com/tract/brethren-of-the-lord The Catholic Encyclopedia notes this is now the view adopted by most of the Protestant exegetes that they were Mary's sons, and argues against it. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/brethren-of-the-lord Jerome argues the same point. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3007.htm

**v. 13**
- Ryle notes Jesus honoured the Old Testament feasts even when unworthy men ran them. He says the exact number of Passovers Jesus kept is disputed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
- Utley counts three Passovers in John, and possibly a fourth, so the ministry lasted at least three years. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2

**vv. 14–16**
- The traders filled the Court of the Gentiles, the only place Gentiles could pray, and their dishonesty made it worse (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- **One cleansing or two?**
  - **Two:** Guzik and Precept Austin take this as an early cleansing, separate from the one in Holy Week in the other three Gospels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
  - **One, placed early:** Utley says it actually happened in Jesus' last week. John placed it early for theological reasons, with no invented events. https://bible.org/seriespage/john-2
- **Pattern:** Guzik notes the order of the chapter, conversion (water to wine) and then cleansing (the temple), and calls this how Jesus always works in his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/

**v. 17**
- The disciples linked Jesus' zeal to Psalm 69:9. Morris, quoted by Guzik, thinks the action probably did not end the trading for good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/

**v. 18**
- Ryle notes some angrily demanded a sign from the one showing zeal for purity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary

**vv. 19–21**
- Jesus meant his body and may have pointed to himself. The irony is that the leaders themselves would bring about the fulfilment (Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-2/
- Guzik adds that the body of Jesus is still a temple, citing Ephesians 2 and 1 Peter 2. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jhn/Jhn_2.cfm
- (I found nothing specific on v. 20.)

**v. 22**
- The disciples only understood Jesus' words after the resurrection: first they remembered, then they believed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary

**vv. 23–25**
- The KJV Bible Commentary (Hindson) calls these people believers in name only. They wanted miracles and saw Jesus as a wonder-worker, without saving faith, so he did not entrust himself to them. Ryle, also quoted there, lists the passage's people: some profit from the temple, some angrily demand a sign, some show false faith, and a few believe with weak faith. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-2-commentary
